proof:
# Equality of mixed depths forces supporting-facet flux outside the base slab

Let d>=1 and let mu be the sum of d-dimensional volume on finitely
many positive full-dimensional convex fibers K_z, z in P subset Z^n.
Write M=mu(S)>0 and let D(y) be normalized ambient closed-halfspace
depth. When invoking interpolation membership below, assume these
fibers are induced by a convex body. No rationality or smoothness
assumption is made.

The main conclusion is an exact necessary inequality for an equality
cap. It implies strict interpolation in every integer dimension for
fibers without positive-area supporting facets, and supplies a finite
balanced circuit constraint at a global-maximizer plateau. It does
NOT exclude such a plateau for arbitrary faceted fibers.

## 1. Attaining caps and equality along a segment

At a point in the interior of a positive fiber, depth is attained by
a nonvertical through-point cap. Here are the needed details. A
vertical through-point cap can be approximated on the finite base
set by nonvertical caps which contain the point and whose limiting
mass is no greater: tilt its vertical normal by an arbitrarily
small nonzero continuous normal. Fibers of strict vertical sign
are eventually wholly in or out; zero-sign fibers contribute at
most their original full mass. Any containing nonvertical cap may
be translated parallel until its boundary passes through the point.

Normalize its continuous normal to norm one. A minimizing sequence
through an anchor (j,x) can be written

  a_k.(z-j)+u_k.(X-x)>=0,  |u_k|=1.

Pass to u_k->u and to extended-real limits of all the finitely many
numbers a_k.(z-j). Let I be the indices with finite limits and let
E span their vectors z-j. On E the restrictions of a_k converge
to a linear functional l, since they converge on a spanning subset
and preserve every linear relation. Extend l to vanish on E^perp.
Replace a_k by a_k-P_E a_k+l. This fixes every finite-index value
at its exact limit and changes all other evaluations by quantities
tending to zero, so their divergence signs are unchanged. For one
sufficiently large k, every divergent-index evaluation dominates
all |u.(X-x)| on its bounded fiber, with the required sign.
Use this finite modified a_k and the limiting unit normal u.
The resulting ONE ambient cap has the exact limiting traces on
every bounded fiber and still passes through the anchor. At the
finite-index fibers, indicator convergence fails only on a
continuous hyperplane of d-volume zero; divergent fibers tend
uniformly to full or empty. Thus its mass is the limiting infimum.
This proves attainment without bounding the original integer
coefficients. It is the anchored form of the finite-threshold
saturation lemma in Section 1 of
`candidate b989614dc4f86228`.

Suppose y_e=(p_e,x_e), e=0,1, are interior points of their positive
fibers, p_0!=p_1, and both have positive depth. If an interior
segment point y=(1-t)y_0+t y_1 has integer base, convexity puts it
in the interior of its own positive fiber: Minkowski interpolation
of the two fiber-interior balls gives a ball there.

Set alpha=min(D(y_0),D(y_1)). Quasiconcavity gives D(y)>=alpha.
If equality holds, an attaining cap H at y must have BOTH endpoints
on its boundary. Indeed its affine margin averages to zero at y.
If an endpoint margin were positive, translating the cap boundary
parallel through that endpoint would strictly remove a positive
volume slab in that endpoint's own fiber, contradicting its depth
lower bound alpha. If neither margin is positive, their zero
weighted average forces both to vanish. Thus H is minimizing at
both endpoints, and both endpoint depths equal alpha as well.

Positive-depth points of a convex fiber family are fiber-interior
points. For a boundary point of a positive fiber, a supporting
continuous normal u and the finite concave support-height data
h_z=max_(K_z)u.x have an affine majorant touching at its base,
by finite linear-program duality. The corresponding ambient
supporting cap has zero d-volume at every fiber. The treatment of
zero-volume original fibers is the separate positive-depth lemma
in Section 5 of the cited critical-cover note; no such fiber is
used as a positive section source here.

## 2. A quantitative inequality for every common equality cap

Let H={L>=0} be a nonvertical cap minimizing depth at BOTH endpoints,
with L(y_0)=L(y_1)=0. Normalize its continuous normal to norm one.
Choose ANY affine base functional h with

  h(p_0)=0,   h(p_1)=1.

Partition the positive-volume fibers meeting its boundary into:

* proper cuts, where the cutting plane meets int K_z;
* supporting cuts, where K_z lies on one side of the plane and
  meets it on its boundary.

Let s_z be the full continuous (d-1)-dimensional section measure;
for d=1 this is H_0=1 for every nonempty section. Put

  A=sum_(proper z) s_z >0,
  B_z=s_z for each supporting z,
  m=sum_(proper z) h(z)s_z.

Both endpoint fibers are proper, so A is strictly positive. The
exact necessary inequality is

  A <= sum_(supporting z) B_z dist(h(z),[0,1]).            (1)

To prove it, for e=0,1 pivot the cap by the one-parameter margins

  L_e,t(z,x)=L(z,x)+t[h(z)-h(p_e)].

It still passes through y_e. Its mass therefore has a local minimum
at t=0. At a proper section, the derivative is
[h(z)-h(p_e)]s_z. At a supporting section, the two one-sided
derivatives are zero and [h(z)-h(p_e)]B_z, in the appropriate order.
These are exact one-dimensional coarea derivatives, including a
supporting facet. The section density is continuous at a proper
cut. At a supporting cut its one-sided limit equals the supporting
section measure: compactness gives the upper limit, and convex
interpolation with an interior point supplies scaled copies of the
supporting section for the lower limit. The statement also holds
for intervals when d=1. Fibers not meeting the plane have zero
derivative, and zero-area supporting sections contribute zero.

Since the left derivative is nonpositive and the right derivative
nonnegative at a local minimum, a convex combination of these two
derivatives is zero. Hence there are effective weights
theta_z^e in [0,1] on the supporting cuts with

  m+sum_z theta_z^0 B_z h(z)=0,
  m-A+sum_z theta_z^1 B_z[h(z)-1]=0.                     (2)

The weights need not be chosen independently or consistently
between the two endpoints. Each set separately comes from its
actual one-dimensional cap perturbation, which is all the proof
uses. Subtracting the equations gives

  A=sum_z B_z[theta_z^1(h(z)-1)-theta_z^0 h(z)]
   <=sum_z B_z[(h(z)-1)_++(-h(z))_+].

The last bracket is precisely dist(h(z),[0,1]), proving (1).
There is no interchange of a maximum and a fiber sum.

### 2.1 The ambient affine extension

The same argument allows ANY ambient affine functional h(w) with
h(y_0)=0,h(y_1)=1. Its exact form is

  A <= sum_(supporting z)
          int_(K_z intersect {L=0}) dist(h(z,x),[0,1])
                                             dH_(d-1)(x). (1a)

Here A is again the full proper-section coarea mass. This includes
distinct continuous endpoints in the SAME integer fiber.

For completeness, pivot with L+epsilon(h-h(y_e)); its continuous
normal remains nonzero for small epsilon, and need not be
renormalized because positive rescaling would not change the cap.
In continuous orthonormal coordinates at a fixed fiber write the
original unit-normal margin as t and write
h=h_0(z,xi)+b t. The new threshold is

  t >= -epsilon[h_0(z,xi)-h(y_e)]/(1+epsilon b).

At a proper section the derivative is the integral of
h_0-h(y_e) over that section. If the body lies on t<=0, its
supporting-section right derivative is the integral of
(h_0-h(y_e))_+ and its left derivative is the integral of
min(h_0-h(y_e),0). If the body lies on t>=0, the right and left
formulas are interchanged. These formulas follow by slicing in
t and dominated convergence: on the relative interior of a
positive-area supporting face the nearby one-sided slice
indicators converge to its indicator, and its relative boundary
is null. A zero-area face contributes zero, since the enclosing
slab has volume o(|epsilon|). At a proper section its relative
boundary is likewise null. All coefficients and source fibers
are bounded, providing a common integrable bound. For d=1 the
same calculation is the one-dimensional interval endpoint rule.

Interpolation of the two one-sided derivatives at each endpoint
now supplies measurable theta_e(z,x) in [0,1] on supporting
sections. The two identities (2) hold with supporting sums
replaced by these integrals, and with m the proper-section
integral of h. Pointwise maximization of
theta_1(h-1)-theta_0 h gives dist(h,[0,1]), proving (1a).
This keeps one consistent trace selection for each endpoint's
actual perturbation; components are not chosen independently.

## 3. Two rigorous strict-interpolation consequences

First, suppose d>=2 and every positive fiber has zero
(d-1)-dimensional measure on every supporting hyperplane. This
includes strictly convex fibers, but does not require smoothness.
Then the right side of (1) is zero for every putative equality cap.
Consequently every intermediate integer segment point satisfies

  D((1-t)y_0+t y_1)>min(D(y_0),D(y_1))                    (3)

whenever the endpoint bases are distinct and the depths positive.
The ambient extension (1a) gives the same strict assertion for
ANY two distinct positive-depth endpoints whenever the intermediate
point is mixed-integer, including endpoints in the same fiber.
The attainment and equality-cap argument of Section 1 is unchanged
in that case. Thus in this class there is at most one global
maximizing POINT in each integer parity class, and at most 2^n
such points in total. The condition excludes facets and is not an
assumption permitted in a full proof of OC; this is a structural
subclass theorem only.

Second, without any regularity assumption and for every d>=1,
(3) holds whenever some affine h normalized at the two endpoints
satisfies 0<=h(z)<=1 for all positive-volume base indices z.
The endpoints then lie on opposite supporting sides of a slab
containing the positive-base projection. Again (1) has zero
right side. Thus a hypothetical equal-depth global pair cannot
be an antipodal pair of this kind.

More generally (1) is an explicit necessary exterior-facet budget:
at least one positive-area supporting section must occur at a
base OUTSIDE the endpoint slab, and its weighted exterior distance
must pay for the entire proper-section measure A.

## 4. A finite balanced circuit at a global plateau

Now suppose beta>0 is the GLOBAL maximum depth on S and both
y_0,y_1 attain beta, with DISTINCT integer bases p_0!=p_1 as in
Section 1. Suppose an interior segment point y has integer base.
Quasiconcavity and global maximality give D(y)=beta. The distinct-base
hypothesis is retained in this section, in particular for its base-affine
shear below; the earlier ambient-affine same-base extension does not
permit identifying two distinct continuous points by that shear.

Use the exact finite CLOSED critical-cap cover from Section 2 of
`candidate b989614dc4f86228`. In the mixed-convex
setting it has at most 2^n(d+1) nonvertical caps, each of mass at
most beta M, covering every point of S. Its proof uses the ordinary
finite mixed-Helly cover and the proved finite-threshold saturation;
it does not use OC. No exact representation of every depth-region
facet is asserted or needed.

Every cover cap containing y has mass exactly beta M and, by the
strict slab argument in Section 1, has both endpoints on its
boundary. The finitely many cover caps not containing y exclude
a neighborhood of y. As y is in the interior of its own fiber,
the containing caps must therefore cover a continuous ball around
y within that fiber. Their boundaries pass through y, so their
homogeneous continuous restrictions cover ALL R^d.

It follows that their continuous normals contain a strictly
positive balanced minimal circuit: otherwise strict separation
of zero from their convex hull gives a direction missed by every
cap. A minimal subset containing zero in its convex hull has
positive coefficients and at most d+1 members, with rank one
less than its cardinality. Each of these actual critical caps
simultaneously satisfies (1), for the SAME functional h and the
SAME endpoint slab.

For clarity, their integer coefficients also obey an exact
geometric constraint. Make the allowed fiber shear

  x'=x-x_0-h(z)(x_1-x_0).

Both endpoint continuous coordinates become zero. Every common
equality cap still has the same continuous normal, and its
integer coefficient a_i' satisfies

  a_i'.(p_1-p_0)=0.                                     (4)

The shear fixes all base indices, preserves all fiber volumes,
and preserves the full ambient halfspace family. Equations
(1) and (4), together with the positive continuous-normal
balance, are necessary simultaneous constraints. We do not
infer from them that the integer displacement vanishes.

For polytopal fibers, (1) implies that each circuit normal is
parallel, in one of its two orientations, to an actual positive-area
facet of some original fiber outside the slab. Thus a global
plateau can use only these finitely many supporting-facet directions.
This is a finite incidence restriction, not a proof that no such
balanced family exists.

## 5. Calibration and the remaining obstruction

The layered-cube example in
`candidate f32902d5e2b99bcc`
has endpoints p_0=-e_1,p_1=e_1, h(z)=(z_1+1)/2 and cap x<=0.
There are 3^n proper sections, each of H_0 measure one, while the
only supporting indices outside the slab are z_1=+-2. Each side
has 5^(n-1) such indices and exterior distance 1/2. Therefore

  A=3^n,    sum B_z dist(h(z),[0,1])=5^(n-1).             (5)

The necessary inequality first becomes possible at n=4:
3,9,27 exceed 1,5,25, whereas 81<125. This is an exact
calibration of why that arbitrary-positive-depth plateau cannot
occur in its lower-dimensional versions. That example's points
are not global maximizers, so it does not settle the stronger
question addressed in Section 4.

For arbitrary faceted fibers, the exterior terms in (1) can be
large. Forgetting the common base-displacement direction in (4)
produces a marginal density which is a SUM of fiber indicators,
not uniform volume on a convex fiber. Neither its required
log-concavity nor a sharp projected depth inequality has been
proved. The simultaneous balanced-circuit and exterior-facet
constraints do not presently close that gap. No global
same-parity exclusion or global-maximizer counterexample is
claimed here.

Subsequent exact result: the newer note
`candidate 5cb6b3de949f5208` constructs
an actual global plateau at three consecutive integer bases for n=2
and every d>=1. Thus arbitrary-faceted global same-parity exclusion
is false. The depth in that example is 1/3, above the OC target;
all flux inequalities and the facet-free subclass conclusions in
this note remain valid. The orientation-resolved strengthening is
recorded in `candidate e81d0f726880ea4a`.
